Honestly, every device out there will stutter at one point or another. I have friends with iPhone 6's and Galaxy S6's, and they all stutter from time to time. The real differentiating factor is that the Moto X released with the iPhone 5, and if you compare the two the Moto X has less stutter, better battery, and an on par camera with the iPhone 5. I'm a power user too, so switching to iPhone isn't an option unless I want to lose all the neat things my phone does. All that to say, I love it :D

Nexus 6 running M developer preview. Bugs from being a preview aside, I really enjoy most of the changes they have added to M, it feels like a refined version of Lollipop. The device is probably a little large for me, but it is still very usable. I would prefer a device 5" to 5 1/2", but this device is fine if you want a lot of screen real estate. I wouldn't consider upgrading soon because I just recently purchased it, but if Google releases a killer new Nexus 5, I might consider selling it.

LG G2. It's my first flagship device, and I love it. The hardware is all around great, nice display, great performance, great camera (especially compared to my previous phones), I actually find the IR blaster useful, I always thought it was just a stupid gimmick, and the battery is great.

There are some things that I don't like, like the placement of the speaker, which I accidentally cover up a lot, and the software. I was always a stock Android fan, and while I have no problem with LG's skin, IMO it's fairly good looking, has some features that stock Android could borrow, and performance is great, I just simply like stock Android better. And while it's not a slow phone at all, it could be way faster on stock Android.

I'd flash a custom ROM, but then I'll have a worse camera.

So yeah, I'm guessing sooner or later we are going to need to copy /r/socialistprogrammers but until then, there are three big computer/information system issues that concern socialism:

  1. Free Software
  2. Net Neutrality
  3. The Digital Divide.

Free software: https://www.gnu.org/philosophy/free-sw.html

The freedom to run the program as you wish, for any purpose (freedom 0). The freedom to study how the program works, and change it so it does your computing as you wish (freedom 1).Access to the source code is a precondition for this. The freedom to redistribute copies so you can help your neighbor (freedom 2). The freedom to distribute copies of your modified versions to others (freedom 3). By doing this you can give the whole community a chance to benefit from your changes. Access to the source code is a precondition for this

Net Neutrality:

https://www.ocf.berkeley.edu/~raylin/whatisnetneutrality.htm

Digital Divide:

The digital divide describes the haves and have nots of access to information technology. This the the last one not talked about in the liberal media. I think internet access should be a right. So should computer access. I see a bigger problem as the poor routinely connect to the internet via cellphone tablets which have less freedom, and less access to content production tools such as video editors and compilers.

So, I define a computer for this measure as having access to a computer that is readily capable of installing a Free Software compliler and toolchain that will run modern software, with at least 5 MB/s broadband.

A compiler being the metric, because once you have a compiler/toolchain you can start building media editing tools.
Three Directives of the Socialist Computer Nerd
